This page goes with **Chapter 32, Impressionism and Extended Tonality** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ImpressionismAndExtendedTonality.html). Read each section there first.
Pieces are named and described, not reproduced; find them on [IMSLP](https://imslp.org/) or by the listening links.

## 32.1 Modes and other collections

The chapter names three habits of Debussy and Ravel: writing in church modes, adding upper extensions (ninths, elevenths, thirteenths) to chords, and parallelism.
Its examples include the start of Debussy's String Quartet (Phrygian), the Danse profane (Lydian) and the first movement of Ravel's Piano Trio (Dorian).
Hear the collections from any starting note. The whole-tone, pentatonic and octatonic scales are not in the chapter; their use by these composers is
from memory and **unverified** here (Debussy's piano prelude *Voiles* is the usual whole-tone example, [listen](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Debussy+Voiles)).

::: {.pt data-pt="collections" data-coll="lydian"}
:::

The "Different transpositions" row shows why the whole-tone scale (2) and octatonic scale (3) feel tonic-less: starting on another note often gives the same notes.
The "Wash" button plays random notes of the collection with no tune.

## 32.2 Pandiatonicism

Using only the notes of one major scale without making them behave like chords in a key. The book names Stravinsky's *Petrushka* (Fourth Tableau) and Copland's *Appalachian Spring*.
Try the Wash button on a major scale: any notes together sound consonant-ish, and nothing wants to resolve.

## 32.3 Planing, quartal, quintal and secundal chords

**Planing** moves a chord in parallel. Ravel's *Pavane pour une infante défunte* (parallel dominant ninths) and Debussy's *Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun* (parallel sevenths) are the chapter's examples.
**Quartal** chords stack fourths, **quintal** fifths, **secundal** seconds. The book's examples: Schoenberg's Chamber Symphony No. 1, Op. 9 and TV themes (quartal), Bartók's Piano Concerto No. 2, II (quintal).
Choose a shape and hear it slide. In real planing every chord is the same set class; in diatonic planing (white notes) the sizes of the intervals change.

::: {.pt data-pt="planing"}
:::

## 32.4 Polychords

Two chords sounding at once, written one above the other. The Rite of Spring chord is an E&flat; dominant seventh over an F&flat; major triad (Stravinsky, "Dance of the Adolescents"; the button below spells F&flat; as E).

::: {.pt data-pt="polychord"}
:::

## Practice

1. Which collection has the notes C D E F&sharp; G&sharp; A&sharp;?
2. A planed major triad rises by step. What is the Forte name of each chord?
3. What is the set class of a quartal tetrachord (C F B&flat; E&flat;)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

1. The whole-tone scale on C (set class 6-35).
2. 3-11 for each, since real planing keeps the shape exactly.
3. 4-23, (0257).
:::
